title: Sixteen steps
hookLine: the breathing discourse gives sixteen steps in four groups of four

lines: A WHOLE PATH IN SIXTEEN STEPS.
cards: Since you woke up this morning, you've breathed thousands of times, and you didn't have to think about a single one. Breathing happens whether you pay attention or not. And it only ever happens now.
You can't take yesterday's breath, or tomorrow's. Maybe that's why the Pali texts give it a discourse of its own: number 118 in the Middle Length Discourses, the Anapanasati Sutta.
It takes something you do without thinking and turns it into a whole path, in sixteen steps.

teach.b: The discourse opens on a full-moon night at the end of the rainy season. Many monks are gathered, and the Buddha is so pleased with them that he stays another month. Then he teaches this.
The standard explanation splits today's word, anapanasati, in three. Ana: breathing in. Apana: breathing out.
Sati: mindfulness. It begins simply. A person goes to a forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty room.
Sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front. Mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.
Then come sixteen steps, in four groups of four.
The first four are about the body: the long breath, the short breath, the whole body, calming the body. The second four, feeling: joy, ease, noticing feelings, calming them.
The third four, the mind: knowing it, gladdening it, steadying it, freeing it. The last four, seeing clearly: change, fading, ending, letting go.

teach.h: EVERY STEP RIDES ON ONE BREATH.
teach.b: Body, feeling, mind, and the way things are: a map of the whole inner life, riding on one breath.
And the discourse makes a big claim: this simple practice, developed and made much of, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, and those lead on to awakening.
Over the next ten days you'll walk these steps a few at a time. They aren't meant to be finished in a week. But every one begins where you already are: breathing in, breathing out.

how: Anapanasati is taught in Theravada monasteries and in meditation centers in many countries, and practice begins with simply knowing the in-breath and the out-breath.

o: a breathing exercise to slow the heart
mindfulness of breathing in and out
holding the breath to quiet the mind

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: it means mindfulness of breathing: you know the breath rather than change it.
the discourse's sixteen steps come in four groups of four
body, feeling, mind, and seeing clearly.
MN 118 opens on a full-moon night at the end of the rains
the Buddha is so pleased with the gathered monks that he stays another month.

games.q: you're a monk, and the Buddha is about to teach mindfulness of breathing. where does the discourse say to begin?
o: in a forest, at a tree or an empty room, sitting upright.
games.why: the discourse begins with the forest, the foot of a tree or an empty place: legs crossed, body upright, mindfulness set in front.

practice: Sit the way the discourse describes, as best you can: upright but not stiff, chair or cushion, attention resting where the breath is easiest to feel, the nostrils, the upper lip or the chest.
Don't change the breath, just know it: breathing in, you know you're breathing in; breathing out, you know you're breathing out. When the mind wanders, and it will, come back to the next breath.

wordCard.voice: Anapanasati. Mindfulness of breathing in and out, taught in sixteen steps.

orig.note: Pali: mindfulness (sati) of breathing in and out (ana-apana).

carryVoice: Your line: sixteen steps, one breath. The whole path fits inside something you already do. Day one hundred and seven, done.
